## Abstract

A  Time  Correlated  Single  Photon  Counting  (TCSPC)  system  was developed  at  Sandia  National  Laboratories  capable  of  measuring scintillator pulse shapes in response to neutron and gamma irradiation with  resolution  of approximately 30  ps.  The  system  was  designed  to minimize  the  primary  contributors  to  the  temporal  uncertainty  in  a TCSPC  measurement.  The  results  of  this  research  and  development effort will be presented along with preliminary measurements of the temporal  response  of  a  series  of  fast  plastic  scintillators.  These  data provide  fundamental  inputs  for  likelihood  reconstruction  approaches to  neutron  imaging  and  high-fidelity  models  of  system  response  for detectors employing these fast plastic scintillators.

## Why TCSPC

• Why not just couple the PMT210 to the scintillator? • MCPs suffer from gain fluctuations, and long recovery time

• Not guaranteed to accurately capture a scintillation pulse when closely coupled • These concerns are mitigated by loosely coupling the PMT210 to count single

photons • Easy to saturate? • Long dead time because of high resistance? • When an MCP is irradiated by a pulsed electron current, a positive charge

is generated at the MCP output end in accordance with the released electron current. This phenomenon deforms the potential distribution and weakens the electric fields so that the subsequenct electron multiplication is suppressed. • saturation

# Hepatocyte Rho-associated kinase signaling is required for mice to survive experimental porphyria-associated liver injury

**Authors:** Jessica M Herrera; Yun Weng; Tyler J Lieberthal; Marcus Paoletti; Tammy T Chang

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Surgery, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, California, USA | 2UCSF/UC Berkeley Joint Graduate Program in Bioengineering, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, California, USA | 3Liver Center, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, California, USA

## Abstract

Rho-associated kinases 1 and 2 (ROCK1 and ROCK2) regulate critical cell functions, including actomyosin contractility, apoptosis, and proliferation. Some studies suggest that ROCK inhibition may serve as a treatment for liver fibrosis. More investigation is needed to understand the role of hepatocyte ROCK signaling in vivo, especially in the context of profibrotic liver injury.

Rock1 fl/fl , Rock2 fl/fl , and Rock1 fl/fl ; Rock2 fl/fl mice were given adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8)-thyroid hormone-binding globulin (TBG)-Cre to produce targeted gene deletion in hepatocytes, or given AAV8-TBG-Null to generate littermate controls (WT). Mice were then placed on a 0.1% 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC) diet to induce liver injury.

Upon DDC-induced liver injury, mice with hepatocyte-specific deletion of ROCK1 alone (R1 KO) or ROCK2 alone (R2 KO) demonstrated minimal differences compared to WT. In contrast, mice with hepatocyte-specific deletion of both ROCK1 and ROCK2 (DKO) showed pervasive early mortality, increased hepatocellular injury, and decreased hepatic function. DDC-injured DKO mice demonstrated markedly distorted liver histology characterized by large cavities in the parenchyma. RNA-seq analysis showed upregulation of cell death, inflammatory, and profibrotic pathways in DDC-injured DKO liver as compared to DDC-injured WT liver. Cdkn1a (gene encoding p21) was one of the most highly upregulated genes in the DKO liver in response to DDC-induced injury. Correspondingly, there was increased hepatocyte nuclear localization of p21 and expression of cleaved caspase-3 in DDC-injured DKO liver, consistent with the activation of p21-mediated caspase-3–dependent apoptotic cell death pathways. ROCK1/ROCK2-deficient primary hepatocytes demonstrated increased susceptibility to both caspase-3–mediated apoptosis and caspase-3–independent forms of cell death in a cell intrinsic manner.

ROCK signaling plays a critical role in mediating hepatocyte cell survival pathways in response to liver injury.

Keywords: cell death, DDC, fibrosis, p21, ROCK

## INTRODUCTION

Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) is a serine/threonine protein kinase that regulates actin-myosin cytoskeletal dynamics and key cellular functions, including apoptosis, metabolism, proliferation, and migration.1 Inhibition of ROCK has been shown to prevent and/or improve pulmonary,2,3,4,5 cardiac,6,7 renal,8,9,10 and hepatic11,12,13,14 fibrosis in animal models. Accordingly, there is significant interest in developing pharmacological inhibitors that target ROCK. There are currently 4 such small molecule inhibitors: fasudil, ripasudil, netarsudil, and belumosudil, which are FDA-approved for the treatment of various diseases in the United States. A phase II trial tested the efficacy of belumosudil in the treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.15 It was within this context of emerging clinical interest in using ROCK inhibition to treat fibrotic diseases that we investigate the effect of hepatocyte-specific ROCK deficiency in fibrotic liver disease.

ROCK has 2 isoforms, ROCK1 and ROCK2, that share 65% homology.1 Some studies suggest that ROCK1 and ROCK2 have distinct functions, whereas others demonstrate that they have redundant and/or compensatory actions. ROCK1 has been shown to primarily regulate stress fiber formation, whereas ROCK2 primarily regulates cofilin phosphorylation.16,17 Systemic ROCK1-deficient mice demonstrated failure of the eyelids and ventral abdomen to close during development,18 whereas systemic ROCK2 deficiency resulted in less severe eyelid and abdomen closure defects and increased fetal death due to placental dysfunction.19,20 Experiments using conditional ROCK1 and/or ROCK2 knock-out mouse embryo fibroblasts demonstrated that the 2 isoforms had redundant functions in regulating cell cycle progression, senescence, and tumorigenesis.21 In the liver, genetic deletion of ROCK1 in hepatocytes results in reduced steatosis and steatohepatitis in response to high-fat western-like diets in mice.14,22 On the other hand, administration of a ROCK2-specific inhibitor attenuated thioacetamide-induced liver fibrosis by inhibiting liver macrophage migration and proinflammatory cytokine secretion.13 Administration of Y27632, an inhibitor that targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2, decreases dimethylnitrosamine-induced and carbon tetrachloride–induced fibrosis by inhibiting HSC activation.11,12 Moreover, ROCK signaling is activated in hepatocytes in response to a stiffened fibrotic matrix, which downregulates hepatic functional gene expression.23 Together, findings from these multiple studies indicate that the effects of ROCK1 and ROCK2 activation are context and cell-type–dependent.

To determine the potential effects of ROCK inhibition as a treatment for liver fibrosis, it is important to determine how inhibited ROCK1 and ROCK2 signaling manifest in relevant cell types in various settings. Accordingly, we generated hepatocyte-specific ROCK1-deficient, ROCK2-deficient, and ROCK1/ROCK2 double-deficient mice and challenged them with 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC) that induced an experimental model of porphyria and cholestatic fibrosis. DDC intoxication leads to inhibition of ferrochelatase, a key enzyme in the heme biosynthesis pathway, resulting in intracellular heme depletion and accumulation of its immediate precursor, protoporphyrin-IX. Porphyrins are cytotoxic and induce organelle-specific protein aggregation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and mitochondrial oxidative stress.24,25 Excess porphyrins form crystals and accumulate within bile ductules, causing cholestasis, periportal inflammation, and biliary fibrosis.26 Experiments in this study investigated the role of hepatocyte ROCK signaling in response to DDC-induced cytotoxic and profibrotic injury.

## METHODS

### Mice

C57BL/6 Rock1 fl/fl mice with loxP sites flanking exon 6 and C57BL/6 Rock2 fl/fl mice with loxP sites flanking exons 5–6 were obtained (MRC Harwell Institute) and interbred to produce Rock1 fl/fl; Rock2 fl/fl mice. Six-to-eight-week-old mice were given 2.5 × 1011 viral particles/mouse AAV8-TBG-Cre (AAV.TBG.PI.Cre.rBG; Addgene) by tail vein injection to achieve hepatocyte-specific Rock1 and/or Rock2 deletion. Littermate controls were injected with 2.5 × 1011 viral particles/mouse of AAV8-TBG-Null (pAAV.TBG.PI.Null.bGH; Addgene). Both male and female mice were used in baseline experiments in which mice were on a standard mouse chow diet. To induce cholestatic liver injury, 0.1% wt/wt DDC was mixed in mouse chow (TestDiet) and given to mice ad libitum for up to 4 weeks. Only male mice were given a DDC diet because of known sex-dependent differences in liver injury response to DDC.27,28 All animal experiments were conducted in compliance with ARRIVE guidelines and approved by the UCSF Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol #: AN176137).

### Primary hepatocyte isolation and culture

Hepatocyte isolation was conducted with 2-step perfusion of the liver in situ using Liver Perfusion Media and Liver Digest Media (Thermo Fisher Scientific) followed by separation with a 50% Percoll (GE Healthcare Life Sciences) density gradient. The purity of live hepatocytes was routinely ≥90% by trypan blue exclusion. Hepatocytes were cultured in 5% fetal calf serum (Hyclone) in DMEM supplemented with l-glutamine, antibiotics, and insulin-transferrin-selenium (Mediatech).

### High-throughput RNA sequencing

RNA extraction was conducted with the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Library construction, quality control, sequence alignment, and high-throughput sequencing were performed by Novogene with their standard protocol. High-throughput sequencing was completed on the Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform. STAR alignment software was used to map the quality-controlled reads to the mouse reference genome (mm10). DESeq2 normalized counts (Bioconductor) were used to perform differential gene expression and clustering analyses using GeneSpring GX v14.9 (Agilent Technologies). We used moderated t tests with corrected p < 0.05 to determine differential gene expression between WT and DKO mice. A heatmap using hierarchical clustering based on both entities and conditions on normalized intensity values was generated using a Euclidean similarity measure and Ward’s linkage. The MINSEQE-compliant data set is accessible through the GEO public repository, accession #: GSE235163. RNA-seq data is deposited in the GEO public repository, accession #: GSE235163.

### Statistical analyses

Prism v9.0 (GraphPad) was used to perform statistical analyses, including Kaplan-Meier survival log-rank tests, 1-way ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey's HSD tests, 2-way ANOVA with post-hoc Fisher's LSD tests, and 2-tailed Student's t tests.

Please see Supplemental Methods for additional details, http://links.lww.com/HC9/B874.

## RESULTS

### Administration of adeno-associated virus serotype 8-thyroid hormone-binding globulin-Cre (AAV8-TBG-Cre) induced efficient hepatocyte-specific deletion of Rock1(R1 KO), Rock2 (R2 KO), or both Rock1 and Rock2 (DKO) in Rock1fl/fl , Rock2fl/fl , and Rock1fl/fl; Rock2fl/fl mice, respectively

We obtained Rock1 fl/fl mice and Rock2 fl/fl mice on the C57BL/6 background21 and interbred them to produce Rock1 fl/fl ;Rock2 fl/fl mice. Male and female adult mice, 6–8 weeks of age, were intravenously injected with AAV8-TBG-Cre to achieve targeted gene deletion of Rock1 and/or Rock2 in hepatocytes. Control littermates were injected with viral vectors that did not contain Cre recombinase (AAV8-TBG-Null). To verify that we achieved efficient hepatocyte-specific gene deletion, we determined ROCK1/ROCK2 protein and mRNA expression in whole liver tissues as well as ﻿purified hepatocytes isolated by 2-step perfusion and density gradient separation. As demonstrated by control mice given AAV8-TBG-Null, whole liver tissues and isolated hepatocytes normally express both ROCK1 and ROCK2 (Figures 1A, B). Two weeks after AAV8-TBG-Cre injection, compared to littermates given AAV8-TBG-Null, liver tissues of Rock1 fl/fl mice showed reduced expression of ROCK1, and liver tissues of Rock2 fl/fl mice showed reduced expression of ROCK2 (Figure 1A). In Rock1 fl/fl ;Rock2 fl/fl mice, protein expression of ROCK1 in both whole liver tissues and isolated hepatocytes was routinely reduced to ~≤20% of control levels (Figures 1B, C). In comparison, ROCK2 protein expression was only reduced to 60% of controls in whole liver tissue, whereas isolated hepatocytes showed decreased ROCK2 expression to <10% of controls (Figures 1B, C). These findings suggest that liver expression of ROCK1 is predominately in hepatocytes, whereas ROCK2 is highly expressed in both hepatocytes and liver non-parenchymal cells. Analysis of Rock1 and Rock2 mRNA expression by quantitative real-time reverse-transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) corroborated the protein expression findings. AAV8-TBG-Cre administration reduced expression of both Rock1 and Rock2 mRNA to 20% of control levels in Rock1 fl/fl ;Rock2 fl/fl whole liver tissues (Figure 1D). In isolated hepatocytes, Rock1 mRNA expression was 20% of controls, and Rock2 mRNA was reduced to <2% of controls (Figure 1D). These data showed that expression of Rock1 and/or Rock2 was efficiently inhibited in adult floxed mice 2 weeks after administration of AAV-TBG-Cre, generating hepatocyte-specific Rock1 −/− (R1 KO), Rock2 −/− (R2 KO), and Rock −/− ;Rock2 −/− (DKO) mice.

### DKO mice with hepatocyte-specific Rock1 and Rock2 deficiency showed mild transient liver injury under baseline conditions

Using 2 weeks after AAV8-TBG-Cre administration as the starting point of induced ROCK deficiency, we observed the mice for an additional 4 weeks on a regular chow diet to determine whether the absence of either or both ROCK isoforms induced abnormalities in the liver without any other perturbations. There were no significant differences in serum levels of ALT between wild-type (WT; littermates given AAV8-TBG-Null), R1 KO, and R2 KO mice (Figure 2A). In contrast, some male and female DKO mice demonstrated increased serum ALT levels (>100 U/L) compared to sex-matched WT littermate controls (Figure 2B). Mild liver injury associated with hepatocyte Rock1 and Rock2 deficiency was transient because, as opposed to male DKO ﻿mice at 6 weeks, male DKO mice at 10 weeks ﻿no longer demonstrated higher ALT levels compared to male WT mice (Figure 2C). Upon histological analysis, WT, R1 KO, and R2 KO mice demonstrated comparable normal-appearing liver parenchyma. The livers of DKO mice with serum ALT >100 U/L showed small, scattered tufts of inflammatory cell infiltrates (Figure 2D). These results suggest that under basal conditions, ROCK signaling in hepatocytes may have a role in maintaining normal liver function and homeostasis.

### In response to DDC-induced liver injury, DKO mice demonstrated significantly greater mortality and more severe liver injury than WT, R1 KO, and R2 KO mice

After administration of viral vectors, mice were maintained on a regular chow diet for 2 weeks to allow deletion of hepatocyte ROCK expression under baseline conditions and then switched to a 0.1% DDC diet ad libitum for an additional 4 weeks. Mice that appeared moribund with poor mobility and/or developed weight loss ≥25% of original body weight were euthanized as humane endpoints. The majority of WT (10 of 19 mice, 53%), R1 KO (4 of 7 mice, 58%), and R2 KO mice (6 of 8 mice, 75%) survived for 4 weeks on the DDC diet. In contrast, all 13 DKO mice died or reached the humane endpoint within 2 weeks of the DDC diet (Figure 3A). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated that DKO survival was significantly poorer than WT, R1 KO, and R2 KO mice. There were no significant differences in survival between WT, R1 KO, and R2 KO mice.

We performed serum liver function tests (LFTs) on WT, R1 KO, and R2 KO mice that survived to the 4-week DDC experimental endpoint (Figure 3B). These mice demonstrated hepatocellular injury with elevated ALT and AST characteristic of DDC-induced liver injury. Alkaline phosphatase (Alk Phos) and total bilirubin (Tbili) were elevated compared to baseline, consistent with concurrent cholestatic injury. R2 KO mice exhibited a trend toward increased ALT, decreased Tbili, and decreased Alk Phos compared to WT and R1 KO, but these differences were not statistically significant.

Because DKO mice demonstrated early mortality at 2 weeks after DDC diet initiation, we analyzed the serum LFTs of a separate cohort of WT and DKO mice at the 2-week timepoint. ALT was elevated in DKO to a lesser extent compared to WT mice, whereas AST was similarly elevated in the 2 groups (Figure 3C). Consequently, the AST/ALT ratio in DKO mice was significantly higher than in WT mice and >1.0, suggesting an altered pattern of hepatocellular injury in DKO mice. Higher AST/ALT ratios ≥1.0 have been associated with fulminant hepatitis, poorer prognosis, and increased fibrosis risk in some disease conditions.29 Tbili was significantly higher in DKO mice compared to WT, suggesting more severe cholestasis. Notably, serum albumin was significantly decreased in DKO compared to WT mice, indicating reduced hepatic synthetic function in DKO mice. Together, these results indicate that ROCK signaling has a critical role in mediating the hepatocyte compensatory survival response to DDC-induced liver injury, and that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may have redundant roles in this response.

### In response to DDC-induced injury, liver tissues of R2 KO mice demonstrated increased porphyrin deposition and similar ﻿ fibrosis compared to WT and R1 KO mice

At the 4-week DDC experimental endpoint, WT, R1 KO, and R2 KO mice were euthanized, and their livers were collected for histologic analysis. In all 3 groups of mice, H&E staining demonstrated periportal inflammation and ductular reaction characteristic of DDC-induced injury26 as well as deposition of porphyrin crystals (dark brown staining) that cause obstructive cholestasis (Figure 4A). Sirius Red staining showed aligned collagen fibers concentrated around periportal areas and surrounding ductular reactions, which are findings typical for DDC-induced biliary fibrosis. Quantification of the porphyrin staining area revealed that there was more porphyrin deposition in R2 KO liver tissue compared to WT and R1 KO liver tissue (Figure 4B). However, the clinical relevance of the increased porphyrin deposition was unclear, because hydroxyproline assay showed comparable collagen content and similar degree of fibrosis between WT, R1 KO, and R2 KO mice (Figure 4C). R2 KO mice showed a trend toward lower serum Tbili and Alk Phos compared to WT and R1 KO (Figure 3B), indicating that increased porphyrin deposition did not correlate with increased cholestasis. Overall, in response to DDC-induced liver injury, R1 KO and R2 KO mice were histologically and phenotypically similar to WT mice.

### DKO mice moribund from DDC-induced liver injury demonstrated large cavities in their liver parenchyma

Cohorts of WT and DKO mice were analyzed at 2 weeks after DDC diet initiation because all DKO mice died or reached the humane endpoint at 2 weeks. The 2-week timepoint is early in the development DDC-induced cholestasis and fibrosis,26 as evidenced by the relatively mild periportal inflammation and collagen deposition in WT mice (Figure 5A). In contrast to the mild signs of histologic liver injury in WT mice, the liver parenchyma of DKO mice were severely distorted with large cavities (Figure 5A). In DKO mice, normal liver lobule architecture was difficult to identify; inflammatory infiltrates appeared to be near periportal zones, and extending into mid-lobular and pericentral areas. Large tissue cavities were located adjacent to inflammatory filtrates and collagen deposits, but also extended beyond these areas. Despite marked abnormalities in DKO liver architecture, the collagen content in WT and DKO livers was comparable (Figure 5B), indicating similar levels of fibrosis. Thus, early mortality and moribund condition of DKO mice on DDC diet correlate with profound liver tissue defects that consist of large cavities throughout the parenchyma.

Elevated bile acid levels in cholestasis are cytotoxic.30 To determine whether increased liver bile acids may contribute to the formation of parenchymal defects in DKO liver, we measured total bile acids in serum and liver of DDC-injured WT and DKO mice (Figure 5C). Overall, serum bile acids were increased in mice given DDC diet compared to chow diet, consistent with DDC-induced cholestasis. DKO mice demonstrated greater serum bile acids than ﻿compared to WT mice in both the baseline chow condition and the DDC-injured condition. In contrast, there was no difference in liver bile acids between WT and DKO mice within either the chow or DDC conditions. These findings suggest that increased serum bile acids in DDC-injured DKO mice, but not liver parenchymal bile acids, may be a contributing factor mediating liver parenchymal injury.

DDC inhibits ferrochelatase (Fech) in the heme synthesis pathway, leading to accumulation of porphyrins that are cytotoxic and cause cholestasis by obstructing bile ductules. We determined the gene expression of several enzymes in the heme synthesis pathway, including Fech, in DDC-injured WT and DKO mice, and found that expression was decreased in DKO mice (Figure 5D), likely manifesting generalized loss of hepatic parenchyma and function in DDC-injured DKO liver.

To further investigate the parenchymal cavities in DKOs, we performed CK19 staining to determine whether the cavities may represent biliary cysts (Figure 5E). There were no CK19+ cholangiocytes lining the parenchymal cavities that would suggest cyst formation in DKO mice. Instead, the DKO parenchymal cavities appeared to be simple voids in the tissue with an abrupt loss of cells. Corroborating these findings, expression levels of mature cholangiocyte markers were either comparable or decreased in DDC-injured DKO liver compared to WT (Figure 5F). Interestingly, the expression of progenitor cholangiocyte markers, especially Jag1, was increased in DKO compared WT (Figure 5G). Together with the clinical data, these results support the hypothesis that large parenchymal cavities in DDC-injured DKO liver represent tissue loss due to massive uncompensated hepatocyte cell death, without expansion of cholangiocytes or formation of biliary cysts.

### RNA-seq analysis showed that DDC-injured DKO liver had decreased function and increased cell death compared to DDC-injured WT liver

To further investigate the mechanisms underlying the striking clinical and histologic outcomes in DKO mice, we performed RNA-seq analysis on the liver tissues of WT and DKO mice 2 weeks after initiating the DDC diet. Gene expression analysis revealed 169 significantly differentially regulated genes between DDC-injured WT and DKO liver (Figure 6A). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) showed that compared to DKO livers, WT liver tissues were enriched for HNF4A and HNF1A target genes as well as hepatic metabolic pathways such as bile acid metabolism, fatty acid metabolism, xenobiotic metabolism, and coagulation (Figure 6B). HNF4A and HNF1A are major master transcriptional regulators of hepatic functional genes.31 These findings suggested that a key difference between DDC-injured WT and DKO liver was that vital hepatic functions were maintained in WT mice, whereas they were significantly diminished in DKO mice. Compared to WT livers, GSEA showed that DKO liver tissues were enriched for the KRAS and p53 pathways as well as pathways related to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, inflammation, and cell death. These findings suggested that DKO livers demonstrated heightened cell survival and cell death signaling, triggering increased inflammatory and profibrotic responses compared to WT. Furthermore, gene ontology (GO) analysis of 2-fold differentially upregulated genes in WT revealed the enriched GO term, “organic acid metabolic process” (GO:0010942), which encompassed genes involved in a broad range of hepatocyte-specific functions (Figure 6C). In contrast, GO analysis of 2-fold upregulated genes in DKO revealed the enriched term, “positive regulation of cell death” (GO:0010942) (Figure 6D). These complementary analyses provided support that in response to DDC-induced liver injury, DKO mice demonstrated reduced hepatic functions and greater cell death compared to WT mice.

Furthermore, we analyzed the expression of validated gene sets enriched in periportal versus pericentral hepatocytes32 in DDC-injured WT and DKO mice. DDC intoxication causes obstructive cholangitis and biliary fibrosis that primarily impact periportal hepatocytes. Our analysis revealed that while some periportal genes were significantly downregulated in DKO mice compared to WT (eg, Cyp2f2, Aldh1b1, and Acly), the periportal gene set was overall comparably expressed between the 2 groups (Figure 6E), suggesting that the effect of periportal hepatocyte injury was similar. In contrast, the entire pericentral gene set was significantly downregulated in DKO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 6F), suggesting that pericentral hepatocytes and their functions were more impacted in DKO mice than in WT. These gene expression findings were consistent with histological findings in which inflammation was limited to periportal zones in WT mice, whereas parenchymal cavities that distorted hepatic lobule architecture in DKO mice extended from periportal into pericentral areas (Figure 5A). Collectively, the clinical, histological, and transcriptomic results indicate that DDC produced more profound and widespread hepatocyte injury and cell death in DKO mice compared to WT mice.

### Proinflammatory and profibrotic genes were more upregulated in DDC-injured DKO liver and corresponded to a broader distribution of infiltrating macrophages and neutrophils throughout the liver lobule

GSEA analysis indicated that proinflammatory and profibrotic pathways were upregulated in DDC-injured DKO liver as compared to DDC-injured WT liver, and we examined the expression of specific genes within these identified pathways. Among the most highly differentially upregulated genes in DKO livers were inflammatory chemokines Ccl2, Ccl7, and Cxcl1 (Figure 7A). Ccl2 and Ccl7 are powerful chemoattractants for monocytes and macrophages; both chemokines bind to the receptor CCR2, which is known to be an important mediator of liver inflammation.33 Cxcl1 is a key chemokine for mobilizing and recruiting neutrophils, and it is produced by hepatocytes in response to the presence of dead cells.34 Accordingly, Cd14, Ccr1, and Il3ra, which are monocyte/macrophage and neutrophil cell markers, were more highly expressed in DDC-injured DKO than in the WT liver (Figure 7B). Upregulation of genes in the DKO liver involved in epithelial-mesenchymal transition, such as Vim and Acta2, showed evidence of increased stellate cell activation (Figure 7C). Expression of early fibrotic extracellular matrix (eg, Lum, Col5a1, and Col5a2)35,36 and key promoters of fibrosis progression such as Spp1 (osteopontin)37 and Ccn2 (connective tissue growth factor)38 were also more highly upregulated in DKO compared to WT (Figures 7D, E). Importantly, immunohistochemistry staining showed that whereas F4/80+ macrophages were relatively restricted to periportal zones in the WT liver, they were increased and more diffusely located throughout the liver lobule in the DKO liver (Figure 7F). Similarly, Ly6G+ neutrophils were concentrated near periportal areas in the WT liver, whereas they were more wide﻿spread throughout the liver lobule in the DKO liver (Figure 7G). These gene expression and histologic results indicate greater activation of proinflammatory/profibrotic pathways and more extensive﻿ inflammatory cell infiltration in the DDC-injured DKO liver.

### Hepatocyte-specific ROCK1/ROCK2 deficiency upregulated Cdkn1a expression and increased activation of cell death pathways in response to DDC-induced liver injury

Through our transcriptomic analysis, we found that Cdkn1a expression was increased nearly 6-fold in DDC-injured DKO liver as compared to DDC-injured WT liver (Figure 8A). Increased Cdkn1a expression was a key driver in several of the hallmark pathways enriched in DDC-injured DKO liver, including the p53 pathway, TNFA NF-κB signaling, and apoptosis. We performed qRT-PCR to determine the expression of Cdkn1a in the livers of WT and DKO mice maintained on a regular chow diet, and we found that Cdkn1a levels were greater in DKO livers than in WT livers under these baseline conditions (Figure 8B). Moreover, DDC intoxication significantly increased the expression of Cdkn1a in both WT and DKO liver, and the increase in Cdkn1a expression in DKO was much greater than in WT. Cdkn1a encodes p21, which is a potent inhibitor of cell cycle progression.39 Under certain conditions, such as bile acid–mediated hepatocyte injury under cholestatic conditions, p21 also promotes apoptosis.30 We found that several key proapoptotic genes were upregulated in DDC-injured DKO liver as compared to DDC-injured WT liver, including Bax and Bak1 (Figure 8C).40 Bcl2l1, also upregulated in DKO liver, has 2 alternate splice forms, and the Bcl-xS splice form is proapoptotic.41 Increased expression of other genes in the apoptosis pathway, including Btg2 42 and Tnfrsf12a,43 gave additional support that apoptotic cell death was increased in DDC-injured DKO livers.

Immunohistochemistry showed markedly increased hepatocyte nuclear staining for p21 in DDC-injured DKO liver, confirming nuclear localization and activation of p21 within hepatocytes (Figure 8D). Cleaved caspase-3 staining of DDC-injured DKO liver showed widespread activation of caspase-3 and hepatocytes in various stages of death and dying (Figure 8E). Caspase-3 is initially cleaved and activated within the cytoplasm and subsequently translocates into the nucleus to carry out effector functions.44 DDC-injured DKO liver demonstrated hepatocytes with cytoplasmic cleaved caspase-3 staining as well as hepatocytes with nuclear cleaved caspase-3 staining. In addition, immunohistochemical staining of DDC-injured DKO liver revealed that HMGB1, a nuclear protein and damage-associated molecular pattern, exhibited increased cytoplasmic localization, which is associated with nonregulated cell death, such as necrosis, as well as regulated cell death, including necroptosis (Figure 8F).45 These data suggest that in response to DDC injury, DKO hepatocytes are more susceptible to both caspase-3–mediated apoptotic cell death as well as caspase-3–independent forms of cell death, including probably nonregulated necrotic cell death.

To determine the impact of elevated p21 expression in DKO hepatocytes on hepatocyte proliferation in response to DDC-induced injury, we performed 3-color immunofluorescence staining of HNF4A, p21, and Ki67 on DDC-injured WT and DKO liver tissues (Figure 8G). We quantified the number of p21+HNF4A+ double-positive nuclei (p21-expressing hepatocytes) and showed that they constituted a significantly greater proportion of hepatocytes (total HNF4A+ nuclei) in the DKO liver compared to the WT liver (Figure 8H). Conversely, the proportion of Ki67+HNF4A+ double-positive nuclei (proliferating hepatocytes) was significantly reduced in the DKO liver compared to the WT liver. Moreover, p21 and Ki67 did not colocalize with each other. These findings suggest that the lack of ROCK1/ROCK2 signaling in hepatocytes induced p21 expression that was associated with decreased hepatocyte proliferation in response to DDC-mediated injury.

Finally, to determine whether increased cell death was cell intrinsic to DKO hepatocytes, we isolated primary hepatocytes from WT and DKO mice and plated the cells on top of collagen gels. Caspase 3/7 activity, indicative of caspase-3–mediated apoptotic cell death, was comparable in WT and DKO hepatocytes cultured in baseline media conditions (Figure 8I). Upon induction of cytotoxicity with 5% DMSO, caspase 3/7 activity was significantly increased in DKO hepatocytes compared to WT hepatocytes, indicating that the loss of ROCK1/ROCK2 signaling directly increased hepatocyte susceptibility to caspase-3–mediated apoptosis. In addition, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release, an indicator of overall cell death, including nonregulated forms of cell death, was increased in DKO hepatocyte cultures in both media control and 5% DMSO conditions compared to WT. These results indicate that the absence of ROCK1/ROCK2 signaling caused hepatocytes to be more vulnerable to both caspase-3–mediated apoptosis and caspase-3–independent forms of cell death.

## DISCUSSION

In this study, we showed that mice deficient in hepatocyte ROCK1 or ROCK2 alone were phenotypically comparable to wild-type mice in their response to DDC-induced liver injury. In contrast, mice with hepatocyte-specific deficiency in both ROCK1 and ROCK2 demonstrated markedly reduced survival, accompanied by greater hepatocellular and cholestatic injury. DDC-injured DKO liver demonstrated profoundly distorted tissue architecture with large parenchymal cavities. RNA-seq analysis revealed increased activation of cell death, inflammatory, and profibrotic pathways in DDC-injured DKO livers. Additional analyses showed that pervasive early mortality of DKO mice after initiation of the DDC diet was associated with increased activation of p21, decreased hepatocyte proliferation, and increased cell death of DKO hepatocytes in response to DDC-induced injury.

These results indicated that hepatocyte ROCK signaling played a vital role in the survival response to DDC-induced liver injury and that ROCK1 and ROCK2 had redundant functions in this context. Our results are consistent with findings in ROCK-deficient embryonic fibroblasts in which loss of both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms led to cell cycle arrest, whereas loss of either isoform alone had no effect.21 Our data had some subtle indications that the effect of hepatocyte-specific ROCK2 deficiency may be distinct. Although DDC-injured R2 KO liver showed increased porphyrin deposition, the clinical significance was unclear because survival of R2 KO mice was comparable to WT and R1 KO, and there were no consistent trends or statistically significant differences in serum LFTs. Previous studies reported that specific inhibition of hepatocyte ROCK1 attenuated steatohepatitis,14,22 whereas specific inhibition of ROCK2 in liver macrophages attenuated thioacetamide-induced liver fibrosis.13 Given the broad effects of the Rho/ROCK pathway, our data, and the data of others, indicate that specific targeting of ROCK1 or ROCK2 in specific cell types and under specific contexts will yield different effects and outcomes.

DDC-injured DKO livers showed markedly increased hepatocyte activation of p21, which is a potent inducer of cell cycle arrest. In hepatic cell lines, p21 promoted ceramide-induced apoptosis by upregulating BAX.46 Relevant to DDC-induced injury, p21 overexpression was shown to promote bile acid–induced apoptosis in primary hepatocytes with activation of cleaved caspase-3.30 DDC produces a mixed-type liver injury in which intracellular porphyrin accumulation causes hepatocellular injury,24,25 while the formation of porphyrin crystals within bile ductules causes cholestatic injury and biliary fibrosis.26 Predominantly cytotoxic models, such as dimethylnitrosamine and carbon tetrachloride, may provide additional insights regarding the role of ROCK signaling in response to liver injury. By deleting ROCK1/ROCK2 specifically in hepatocytes, we demonstrated the critical role of hepatocyte ROCK signaling in mediating survival in response to DDC-induced injury. Previously published work showed that systemic administration of Y27632, which theoretically inhibited ROCK1/ROCK2 in all cell types, decreased fibrosis in dimethylnitrosamine-induced and carbon tetrachloride–induced injury and reduced stellate cell activation.11,12 It is possible that the beneficial effects of Y27632 in ameliorating liver fibrosis were because the dosage level inhibited ROCK signaling in activated stellate cells without significant effect on hepatocytes. Accordingly, safe and effective antifibrotic therapy based on Rho/ROCK pathway blockade may be feasible if inhibition is targeted to non-parenchymal cells and avoids deleterious effects on hepatocytes.

Our findings in DKO mice were﻿ remarkably reminiscent of hepatocyte-specific integrin β1-deficent mice in which 7 days of DDC diet induced hepatocyte p21 activation and severely impaired hepatocyte proliferation.47 No animal fatalities﻿ were﻿ reported at this early timepoint, and mice were allowed to recover from the DDC diet. However, during recovery, the proliferative capacity of integrin β1-deficent hepatocytes was so profoundly restricted that cholangiocytes became facultative stem cells to participate in liver regeneration. Focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and the Rho/ROCK pathway are activated downstream of integrin engagement with the extracellular matrix.48 Our data suggest that p21 activation in integrin β1-deficent hepatocytes may be regulated by ﻿ROCK. Similar to integrin β1-deficent hepatocytes, we showed that p21-mediated cell cycle arrest in ROCK1/ROCK2-deficient hepatocytes severely restricted hepatocyte proliferation. Therefore, inhibited liver regeneration may be a contributing factor to the early mortality of DKO mice in response to DDC intoxication. Several experimental systems have shown that Rho/ROCK activation directly inhibits p21 expression and promotes cell proliferation and/or survival. In NIH-3T3 cells, attachment to fibronectin inhibited p21 expression and induced cyclin D1 expression in a Rho/ROCK-dependent manner.49 In a monocyte cell line, ROCK activation suppressed p21 expression in response to protein kinase C stimulation.50 Taken together, these findings suggest an integrin-Rho/ROCK-p21 pathway for mediating hepatocyte survival/proliferative signals in response to liver injury. Interestingly, the phenotype of hepatocyte-specific FAK-deficient mice treated with DDC is relatively mild compared to that of integrin β1-deficient mice and ROCK1/ROCK2-deficient mice,28 suggesting that the lack of hepatocyte FAK signaling may be compensated by other integrin-associated tyrosine kinases, whereas the loss of ROCK signaling cannot be replaced or compensated.

In conclusion, our results indicate that hepatocyte ROCK signaling has an essential role in mediating survival in response to DDC-induced injury. Our findings suggest that efforts to inhibit ROCK signaling as a treatment for liver fibrotic diseases should proceed with caution. ROCK inhibition may be an effective strategy if targeted to non-parenchymal cell types such as myofibroblasts or inflammatory macrophages. However, the therapeutic window must be carefully calibrated to avoid inducing more severe injury as a consequence of inhibiting ROCK-mediated cell survival pathways in hepatocytes.
